claims.text: The initial alloy is an as-cast, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
The initial alloy contains both solid-solution regions and dispersed intermetallic phases.
Thermal or environmental exposure drives decomposition of metastable solid-solution regions.
Metastable solid-solution regions decompose into Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Mg-rich intermetallic compounds act as nucleation sites for protective MgO growth.
Preferential oxidation of Mg-rich regions produces a continuous and adherent MgO barrier.
The continuous MgO barrier improves high-temperature oxidation resistance by modifying subsequent oxidation kinetics.
Phase evolution and MgO formation reduce corrosion rates by disrupting micro-galvanic interactions between phases.
Relative to the as-cast alloy, the thermally aged alloy will have a more uniform and adherent MgO surface layer.
Relative to the as-cast alloy, the thermally aged alloy will exhibit lower corrosion current in a salt environment.
Relative to the as-cast alloy, the thermally aged alloy will exhibit lower oxidation weight gain per unit time.
The as-cast baseline has no significant MgO formation.
The proposed comparison uses an as-cast control and a group aged for approximately 100 hours at 700°C in air.
Corrosion is to be assessed by potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys with density below 6 g/cm3 and exposure temperatures below the melting point.
Composition, processing history, and environmental conditions can change Mg-rich phase kinetics and MgO thickness and continuity.
